programme: GATA3 and PPARG form the core pair — the same GATA3/PPARG axis used clinically to call the luminal-differentiated molecular subtype of bladder cancer — with AR contributing a second steroid/nuclear-receptor input into that differentiation program, and FOSL2 (AP-1) acting as the downstream inflammatory/remodeling effector these nuclear receptors drive (its target list — TGFB1, TGFB3, IL6, IL2, IL5, IL11, MMP13, TIMP1 — is a classic AP-1 stress/remodeling signature).
role_in_a: In Alzheimer's disease the programme is carried mainly by PPARG and FOSL2, not the full quartet: PPARG agonism (pioglitazone) reduces pyroptosis/mitochondrial injury and is modulated by gut-microbiota metabolites, and FOSL2, downstream of FLOT1, drives EphA2-dependent microglial polarization. GATA3's AD evidence here is a GWAS pleiotropy hit for blood pressure/cognition (not mechanistic), and AR's is a cheminformatics drug-repurposing screen, so their AD role is only weakly attested.
role_in_b: In bladder cancer all four factors are directly and independently evidenced: GATA3 and PPARG are the field-standard IHC markers used to call the luminal-differentiated subtype of muscle-invasive disease and predict treatment response, PPARG is additionally stabilized by TRIM28 to actively drive progression, AR signaling (AR-V7) tracks with clinicopathologic behavior, and FOSL2 copy-number changes carry prognostic signal.
shared_axis: If the nuclear-receptor/GATA/AP-1 circuit that sets luminal-vs-basal epithelial identity and immune tone in urothelium also operates in brain myeloid cells, PPARG and its AP-1 partner FOSL2 could be setting an analogous differentiation-like, pro- vs anti-inflammatory polarization state in microglia. That is an inference from the module's known logic in bladder applied to brain, not a documented mechanism connecting the two diseases.
reasoning: PPARG and FOSL2 are independently and mechanistically placed in AD, and GATA3/PPARG/AR/FOSL2 are all independently and more strongly placed in bladder cancer, so the module is real and nameable on each side separately. But no retrieved paper discusses the two diseases together, and nothing in the record (comorbidity, shared risk factor, treatment overlap) makes a bladder-brain pairing obvious, so the coherence of the programme does not extend to a documented or anatomically expected connection between the diseases.

how_to_falsify: In an AD microglial model, apply a PPARG agonist (e.g. pioglitazone) and ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN for GATA3, PPARG, AR and FOSL2 binding; if these factors do not co-occupy the same target loci used to call the luminal bladder-cancer signature (or show no coordinated shift with agonism), the proposed shared circuit does not hold in brain. Corroborating check: query single-cell AD microglial atlases for GATA3/AR differential expression versus controls — if absent, GATA3 and AR are not actually part of an active brain programme and the account reduces to PPARG/FOSL2 alone.
caveats: Tissue pairing is bladder epithelium vs brain, with no anatomical or clinical link asserted in the record. 200 patient-group comparisons come from only 3 independent cohort pairs, so the high recurrence counts reflect repeated subgroup splits of the same underlying cohorts, not 200 independent replications. Single-view exclusions (CIC, SMAD3, HDAC3, GSC, ZBTB10, DMTF1, IRX2, PBX2, GCM1) confirm subgroup-specific artifacts were correctly filtered rather than folded into this story. Tissue-generic exclusions (notably NOTCH1 and NR3C1, close relatives of AR/FOSL2's pathway) were stripped before ranking — their absence here is by design, not an oversight, and this account should not reach for them. AHR's retrieved papers were explicitly about an unrelated meaning of the acronym, a reminder that retrieval noise affects this material generally.
